title: Yonáhqôsunuk
summary: The Smith Site near Smith Cove preserves evidence of Indigenous use across more than one season as well as an ancestral resting place. Public descriptions remain broad to protect ancestors, cultural belongings, and archaeological deposits.
map_geometry_source: Broad public orientation point for Smith Cove from OSM/Nominatim and Directus text; not the campsite, burial, or archaeological location.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Manhansett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: The Smith Cove landscape records enduring Indigenous use of Shelter Island across seasons. It also shows why older archaeological reports must be read critically: ancestors and burial belongings are not objects of curiosity, and precise burial information requires protection.
history_content:
Roy Latham's 1957 preliminary report called this place the Smith Site, after a former property owner. He documented sheltered hollows, elevated stone hearths, and coastal food remains, which he interpreted as evidence of both cold-season shelter and warm-season harvesting.

The report also described ancestral burials according to the archaeological practices and language of its time. Exact locations, human-remains descriptions, and inventories of burial belongings are omitted out of respect for ancestors and to protect the place from disturbance.

1
translation_content:
Yonáhqôsunuk is a later commemorative name used for the place. It draws on a Mohegan-language form translated as "at the place where she sews." Roy Latham's 1957 report does not use this name; it refers to the location as the Smith Site.

1
preservation_content: Only the broader Smith Cove landscape is identified. The ancestral resting place and archaeological deposits require protection from disturbance.
artifacts_content: Hundreds of artifacts from the site, along with manuscripts and field notes were donated by Roy Latham to the Southold Indian Museum, maintained by the Incorporated Long Island Chapter, New York State Archaeological Association. Other artifacts include rubbed graphite, Amphibole talc (steatite, a non-local mineral) vessel sherds, similar to vessels found near Orient on the North Fork. [1. John Charles Witek, Bulletin of the Archaeological Society of Connecticut, Nm 53, 1990, pp. 42-3]
